learn.hook: Bridges that grow, a lake with floating islands and a desert of white salt. These are not fairy tales; they are in India!
points: The lesson 'Spectacular Wonders' takes readers on a journey through amazing natural places and shows how to describe them vividly.
Living root bridges of Meghalaya are grown, not built: Khasi and Jaintia communities guide the roots of rubber fig trees across streams until they form strong bridges.
Loktak Lake in Manipur has floating masses of plants and soil called phumdis. On it lies Keibul Lamjao, the only floating national park in the world and the home of the sangai deer.
Lonar Lake in Maharashtra lies in a crater formed when a meteorite struck the Earth. The Great Rann of Kutch in Gujarat is a vast white salt desert.

The Valley of Flowers in Uttarakhand blooms with wildflowers in the monsoon months; the Sundarbans in West Bengal is a mangrove forest, home to the Royal Bengal tiger; the Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat in Madhya Pradesh line the Narmada river.

example.q: Read this original passage: 'At Bhedaghat, the Narmada slips between cliffs of white marble that rise like the walls of a giant's palace. When the moon shines, the rocks glow silver and the water whispers below.' Think it through: name the wonder, its river, and one comparison the writer uses.
steps: The place named is Bhedaghat, famous for its Marble Rocks.
The river named is the Narmada.
The comparison: cliffs 'rise like the walls of a giant's palace' (a simile using 'like').
'The water whispers' is personification too.
example.answer: The Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat on the Narmada; the cliffs are compared to the walls of a giant's palace.

learn.reallife: Many of these places are protected as national parks or World Heritage Sites. When we visit, we keep them clean and follow the rules so they stay wonderful.

games.title: Wonder facts
items: Living root bridges are made from the roots of rubber fig trees.
Communities guide the living roots across streams over many years.
Keibul Lamjao on Loktak Lake is a floating national park.
It rests on phumdis, the floating mats of plants and soil.
Lonar Lake was dug by people for irrigation.
It lies in a crater formed by a meteorite impact.
The Great Rann of Kutch is a salt desert.
Its huge flat land is covered with white salt in the dry season.
The Sundarbans is a mangrove forest.
Its mangroves grow in the salty, tidal waters of the delta.
The Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat stand beside the river Ganga.
They line the Narmada river near Jabalpur in Madhya Pradesh.

quiz.q: Living root bridges are found in which state?
quiz.explain: They are found in Meghalaya, grown by the Khasi and Jaintia communities.
steps: Living root bridges are grown from tree roots by the Khasi and Jaintia communities.
These communities live in Meghalaya.
Answer: Meghalaya
quiz.mistake: Picks a green state without recalling the fact

quiz.q: What are 'phumdis' on Loktak Lake?
options: Floating masses of plants and soil
quiz.explain: Phumdis are floating mats of vegetation and soil, some large enough to carry a national park.
steps: On Loktak Lake, phumdis float on the water.
They are floating masses of plants and soil.
Answer: Floating masses of plants and soil
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the sound of the word

quiz.q: Which animal is the famous resident of Keibul Lamjao National Park?
quiz.explain: The sangai, a deer, lives on the floating phumdis of Loktak Lake.
steps: Keibul Lamjao National Park floats on phumdis of Loktak Lake.
Its famous resident is the sangai deer.
Answer: Sangai deer
quiz.mistake: Mixes it up with animals of other famous parks

quiz.q: How was Lonar Lake in Maharashtra formed?
options: By a meteorite striking the Earth
By a dam on a river
quiz.explain: Lonar Lake fills a crater made by a meteorite impact.
steps: Lonar Lake fills a crater.
The crater was made by a meteorite striking the Earth.
Answer: By a meteorite striking the Earth
quiz.mistake: Assumes every lake is formed by a river or a dam

quiz.q: Read: 'At Bhedaghat, the Narmada slips between cliffs of white marble.' Which river is described?
quiz.explain: The sentence names the Narmada, which flows past the Marble Rocks.
steps: The sentence itself names the river: 'the Narmada slips between cliffs'.
So the river is the Narmada.
Answer: Narmada
quiz.mistake: Does not read the sentence carefully

quiz.q: The Sundarbans is best known for its ___.
options: mangrove forests and Royal Bengal tigers
quiz.explain: The Sundarbans delta has huge mangrove forests and is home to the Royal Bengal tiger.
steps: The Sundarbans delta is covered with mangrove forests.
It is home to the Royal Bengal tiger.
Answer: mangrove forests and Royal Bengal tigers
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the features of different wonders

quiz.q: Which wonder is a vast white salt desert in Gujarat?
quiz.explain: The Great Rann of Kutch is a huge salt desert in Gujarat.
steps: A vast white salt desert in Gujarat.
That is the Great Rann of Kutch.
Answer: Great Rann of Kutch
quiz.mistake: Confuses the salt desert with the Thar sand desert or other places

quiz.q: Which word means 'amazing to look at'?
quiz.explain: 'Spectacular' means wonderful and striking to see, as in 'Spectacular Wonders'.
steps: 'Spectacular' means amazing and striking to see.
Spectator, speculate and special only look similar.
Answer: spectacular
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with 'spectator', a person who watches

teach.ask: Gappu wants to fly on a holiday. Tell him about two natural wonders of India and where they are!
teach.praise: Whee! Root bridges in Meghalaya and the Sundarbans in West Bengal! India's natural wonders are spectacular!
teach.nudge: Name one wonder in the north-east and one somewhere else. Which states are they in?

revise.summary: 'Spectacular Wonders' takes us through amazing natural places in India and shows how to describe them vividly. Each wonder has its own state and special feature.
focus: Match each wonder to its state and feature.
Know phumdis, Keibul Lamjao and the sangai deer.
Find comparisons in a description of a wonder.
remember: Living root bridges (Meghalaya); Loktak Lake with phumdis and Keibul Lamjao, the only floating national park in the world (Manipur).
Lonar Lake (Maharashtra): a crater formed when a meteorite struck the Earth. Great Rann of Kutch (Gujarat): a vast white salt desert.
Valley of Flowers (Uttarakhand); Sundarbans (West Bengal): mangroves, Royal Bengal tiger; Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat on the Narmada (Madhya Pradesh).
traps: Don't assume every lake is formed by a river or dam; Lonar was formed by a meteorite.
Root bridges are grown, not built.
'Spectacular' (amazing to look at) is not 'spectator' (a person who watches).

learn.hook: 'The waterfall was nice' or 'The waterfall thundered down like a river of milk'? Which one can you see and hear?
points: Descriptive writing helps the reader see, hear, smell, touch and taste a place. Use all five senses.
Choose vivid, precise words: 'roared' instead of 'made a noise', 'emerald' instead of 'green', 'tiny' instead of 'small'.
Similes (like/as), metaphors and personification make descriptions memorable: 'The lake was a mirror for the sky.'
Show, don't tell: instead of 'It was cold', write 'Our breath made little clouds and our fingers went numb.'
Organise the description: from near to far, top to bottom, or the order in which you saw things.

example.q: Think it through: Improve this sentence with sensory details: 'The waterfall was big and nice.'
steps: Sight: what does it look like? White water pouring down like milk.
Sound: what can you hear? It thunders.
Touch: what do you feel? Cool spray on your face.
Combine them into one vivid sentence.
example.answer: The waterfall thundered down the cliff like a river of milk, and its cool spray tickled our faces.

learn.reallife: Travel blogs, tourism brochures and your own holiday diary all use descriptive writing to make readers wish they were there.

games.title: Which sense?
items: golden sand dunes
the roar of the waves
soft, wet moss
emerald paddy fields
crickets chirping at night
icy wind on my cheeks
a rainbow over the falls
rough bark of the old banyan

items.text: The river ___ over the rocks after the monsoon.
The hills were covered in ___ tea gardens.
A ___ breeze carried the smell of jasmine.
The snow peaks ___ in the morning sun.

quiz.q: Which sentence is the most descriptive?
options: The beach was good and big.
Silver waves rushed over the warm, golden sand.
quiz.explain: It uses colour, movement and touch (silver, rushed, warm, golden), so the reader can picture it.
steps: Descriptive writing uses details of the senses.
'Silver waves rushed over the warm, golden sand' has colour, movement and touch.
Answer: Silver waves rushed over the warm, golden sand.
quiz.mistake: Thinks general words like 'nice' are descriptive

quiz.q: Which detail appeals to the sense of smell?
quiz.explain: Fragrance is a smell. The others are about sight, touch and sound.
steps: Match each detail to a sense: pine trees (sight), cold water (touch), cuckoo (sound).
Fragrance of wet earth is a smell.
Answer: the fragrance of wet earth
quiz.mistake: Does not link details to the senses

quiz.q: Read: 'The lake was a mirror for the sky.' This is a ___.
quiz.explain: It compares the lake to a mirror directly, without 'like' or 'as'.
steps: The lake is compared to a mirror directly, without 'like' or 'as'.
That is a metaphor.
Answer: metaphor
quiz.mistake: Calls every comparison a simile

quiz.q: Which sentence 'shows' instead of 'tells' that it was cold?
options: Our breath made little clouds, and our fingers went numb.
quiz.explain: It lets the reader feel the cold through details, without just saying 'cold'.
steps: 'Showing' gives details that let the reader feel it.
Breath making clouds and numb fingers show cold without saying 'cold'.
Answer: Our breath made little clouds, and our fingers went numb.
quiz.mistake: Thinks repeating a word makes it descriptive

quiz.q: Which word is a more vivid choice than 'walked slowly'?
quiz.explain: 'Strolled' paints a picture of walking slowly and calmly.
steps: A vivid verb paints a picture in one word.
'Strolled' means walked slowly and calmly.
Answer: strolled
quiz.mistake: Chooses a general verb

quiz.q: Read: 'The wind whistled through the valley.' Which sense does this detail appeal to?
quiz.explain: 'Whistled' is something you hear.
steps: 'Whistled' is something you hear.
So it appeals to sound.
Answer: Sound
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the sound word

quiz.q: Which is a good way to organise a description of a waterfall?
options: From the top of the falls down to the pool
Only list the names of rocks
quiz.explain: Describing top to bottom (or near to far) helps the reader follow the picture.
steps: A clear order helps the reader follow the picture.
For a waterfall, describe from the top of the falls down to the pool.
Answer: From the top of the falls down to the pool
quiz.mistake: Does not plan the order of a description

quiz.q: Which adjective best replaces 'very big' in 'a very big mountain'?
quiz.explain: 'Massive' means very large and solid.
steps: 'Very big' can be replaced by one strong adjective.
'Massive' means very large and solid.
Answer: massive
quiz.mistake: Picks a word that does not mean large

teach.ask: Gappu wrote: 'The hill was nice.' His teacher wants more. How can he describe the hill better?
teach.praise: Oh, I can see it now! Use the senses, vivid words and a simile, and the hill comes alive!
teach.nudge: What can you see, hear or feel on the hill? Can you compare it to something?

revise.summary: Descriptive writing helps the reader see, hear, smell, touch and taste a place. Use vivid, precise words, figures of speech, 'show, don't tell', and a clear order.
focus: Use details for all five senses.
Replace general words with vivid, precise ones.
Show, don't tell, and organise the description.
remember: Show, don't tell: instead of 'It was cold', write 'Our breath made little clouds and our fingers went numb.'
Organise from near to far, top to bottom, or in the order you saw things.
traps: Don't use general words like 'nice' or 'big'; choose precise ones like 'massive'.
Don't call every comparison a simile: 'The lake was a mirror for the sky' is a metaphor.
Don't describe in a random order; plan it.

learn.hook: Does a boat sail across the lake, through the lake or along the lake? One little word changes the whole picture!
points: Prepositions show the position or movement of something in relation to something else.

across = from one side to the other of a surface (across the river); through = from one end to the other inside something (through the tunnel, through the forest); along = following the length of something (along the beach).
in = inside (in the box); into = movement to the inside (jumped into the lake). on = resting on a surface; onto = movement to a surface.
between = with two things on either side; among = surrounded by many (among the trees).
beside = next to (sat beside the lake); besides = in addition to (Besides tigers, the Sundarbans has crocodiles).

example.q: Think it through: Choose the right prepositions: 'The train went ___ (through/across) a long tunnel and then ran ___ (along/among) the river for an hour.'
steps: A tunnel is something you go inside from one end to the other: through.
Following the length of a river: along.
'Among' needs many things around you, not one river.

learn.reallife: Giving directions uses prepositions: 'Walk along the road, go across the bridge and the shop is beside the post office.'

items.text: We walked ___ the bridge to the other bank.
The deer hid ___ the tall grass.
The hut stands ___ two huge trees.
We cycled ___ the beach road at sunset.
___ the lake, the park also has a rose garden and a small zoo.

games.title: Preposition and picture
pairs: inside, from one end to the other
from one side to the other

quiz.q: Choose the correct preposition: The tiger swam ___ the river to the other bank.
quiz.explain: Going from one side to the other side of a river is 'across'.
steps: From one side of the river to the other side.
The preposition is 'across'.
Answer: across
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'across' with 'through'

quiz.q: Choose the correct preposition: The road goes ___ a thick forest.
quiz.explain: A road inside a forest, from one end to the other, goes through it.
steps: The road is inside the forest, from one end to the other.
The preposition is 'through'.
Answer: through
quiz.mistake: Uses 'among' for passing inside something

quiz.q: Which sentence uses 'besides' correctly?
options: The cup is besides the plate.
quiz.explain: 'Besides' means 'in addition to'. For 'next to', use 'beside'.
steps: 'Beside' means next to; 'besides' means in addition to.
'Besides painting, Asha loves dancing' uses it correctly.
Answer: Besides painting, Asha loves dancing.
quiz.mistake: Confuses beside (next to) with besides (in addition to)

quiz.q: Choose the correct option: The frog jumped ___ the pond.
quiz.explain: 'Into' shows movement from outside to inside.
steps: The frog moves from outside to inside the pond.
That movement is 'into'.
Answer: into
quiz.mistake: Picks a preposition that does not show movement to the inside

quiz.q: Divide the laddoos ___ the two sisters.
quiz.explain: With two people, use 'between'. Use 'among' for more than two.
steps: There are two sisters.
With two, use 'between' ('among' is for more than two).
Answer: between
quiz.mistake: Uses 'among' for two people

quiz.q: Choose the correct option: We walked ___ the bank of the Brahmaputra.
quiz.explain: Walking following the length of a river bank is 'along'.
steps: Walking following the length of the river bank.
The preposition is 'along'.
Answer: along
quiz.mistake: Picks a preposition that does not show direction along a line

quiz.q: What does a preposition show?
options: The relation of a noun to other words, such as place or direction
quiz.explain: Prepositions like on, across and through link a noun or pronoun to the rest of the sentence.
steps: Prepositions like on, across and through link a noun to the rest of the sentence.
They show relations such as place or direction.
Answer: The relation of a noun to other words, such as place or direction
quiz.mistake: Confuses prepositions with verbs or adjectives

quiz.q: Choose the correct option: The cat climbed ___ the roof.
quiz.explain: 'Onto' shows movement to a position on top of a surface.
steps: The cat moves to a position on top of the roof.
That is 'onto'.
Answer: onto
quiz.mistake: Uses 'into' when the movement is onto a surface

teach.ask: Gappu flew across a lake, through a tunnel and along a river. He wants to know: what are these little words, and how are they different?
teach.praise: Swoosh! Prepositions show place and direction: across is side to side, through is inside end to end, along follows the length!
teach.nudge: What do these little words tell us about where I went? What's the difference between across and through?

revise.summary: Prepositions show the position or movement of something in relation to something else. Learn pairs that are easily confused: across/through, in/into, on/onto, between/among, beside/besides.
focus: Choose across, through or along from the meaning.
Use into and onto for movement.
remember: across = from one side to the other of a surface; through = from one end to the other inside something; along = following the length of something.
in = inside; into = movement to the inside; on = resting on a surface; onto = movement to a surface.
between = two things on either side; among = surrounded by many. beside = next to; besides = in addition to.
traps: Don't use 'among' for two people; use 'between'.
Don't confuse 'beside' (next to) with 'besides' (in addition to).
